items.title: Riversimple: What Comes After the Rasa? TNY Design Studio Explores
items.summary: Hidden among the hills of Mid-Wales is a carmaker that has spent more than two decades questioning almost everything about the conventional car. Riversimple isn't chasing enormous batteries, huge horsepower figures or ever-heavier SUVs. Instead, founder Hugo Spowers and his team have pursued an unusually simple idea: build a genuinely lightweight hydrogen-electric…
items.content_html:
For many, the first encounter with Riversimple came in early 2016, when the remarkable Rasa Alpha was unveiled. This was no conventional small car with its petrol engine replaced by a fuel cell. The two-seater had been engineered around efficiency from the outset, with a lightweight composite structure, four in-wheel electric motors and supercapacitors to capture braking energy and support acceleration.

The Alpha used an 8kW hydrogen fuel cell to sustain cruising and replenish stored energy. Riversimple quoted 0–60mph in a little over nine seconds, while the Rasa aimed for a range of roughly 300 miles on just 1.5kg of hydrogen and refuelling measured in minutes rather than hours. These were company targets rather than certified production-car figures.

The next important step was the Rasa Beta, unveiled in 2019 ahead of public trials beginning in 2020. It featured a larger 12kW fuel cell and further refinements to packaging, software and energy management. Trial vehicles gathered valuable experience through projects in Abergavenny and Pembrokeshire, helping transform the Rasa from an experimental concept into a working test bed for Riversimple's wider ambitions.


That brings us to our first Design Studio rendering: a compact, more conventional two-seat Riversimple hatchback. We've retained the brand's flowing surfaces but imagined an everyday shape with a more useful rear end. The result is less experimental than the Rasa. It asks a simple question: if Riversimple wants to bring hydrogen motoring to ordinary drivers, could a small, efficient runabout be the right starting point?

It's not a model invented entirely from thin air. Riversimple's own waiting-list page outlines a proposed two-door, two-seat hatchback with a minimum 330-mile range, a targeted 0–60mph time of 9.5 seconds and a three-minute refuelling time. The company says its proposed subscription and mileage charges are intended to deliver total running costs comparable with a basic petrol MINI. That is a target for the complete cost of motoring, not an announced vehicle purchase price.

Our illustration is an independent TNY interpretation rather than an official Riversimple design. Seen alongside the Morgan LIFECar, Hyrban and two generations of Rasa, it would represent another step in a long line of experimental two-seat concepts. But bringing such a car into production would require more than attractive styling: funding, reliable hydrogen supply, customer support and the capacity to build vehicles consistently all remain crucial.


Riversimple's planned business model is almost as unusual as its cars. Rather than selling the vehicle to the customer, the company intends to retain ownership and charge a fixed monthly subscription plus a mileage rate.

Its proposed package includes insurance, maintenance, tyres and even hydrogen fuel. The driver pays to use the car rather than to buy it outright. Riversimple explains its proposed subscription service on its website.

To understand the Rasa, it's worth travelling back to 2009. The Riversimple Hyrban was a compact, two-seat technology demonstrator developed over the following years to test the company's network-electric approach. Its 6kW powertrain combined a hydrogen fuel cell with supercapacitors, using stored braking energy for bursts of acceleration while the fuel cell handled more constant demands.

Riversimple quoted 0–50mph in around eight seconds and a 50mph cruising capability. They aren't dazzling performance figures by modern standards, but for such a tiny fuel-cell system they represented an important achievement.

The Hyrban demonstrated that remarkable efficiency did not necessarily have to mean an impractically slow car. One example became part of the Science Museum's collection — a fitting recognition of an unusual piece of British engineering.


Riversimple's history also includes one of Britain's most traditional sports-car names. Between 2005 and 2008, Hugo Spowers and collaborators including the Morgan Motor Company worked on the extraordinary Morgan LIFECar — a research project designed to explore how hydrogen-electric technology could meet the expectations of a lightweight sports car.

Revealed at the 2008 Geneva Motor Show, the LIFECar brought together Morgan's distinctive approach to car design with advanced fuel-cell research. It was a development demonstrator, not a showroom model, but it helped show that hydrogen propulsion could be interesting for reasons other than economy alone. Behind that striking bodywork lay the early thinking that would eventually feed into the much smaller Hyrban and Rasa.

Hugo Spowers had established OScar Automotive in the early 2000s after a career in motorsport; the business became Riversimple in 2007. By 2026, the venture's roots therefore stretched back roughly a quarter of a century. It's a remarkably long period of continuous experimentation for a small independent automotive project, and one that makes the company's persistence especially noteworthy.


Our second new rendering asks what happens when Riversimple goes beyond two seats. Until now, its best-known experimental cars have favoured small passenger compartments and very low weight. That's helped efficiency, packaging and aerodynamics, but it also restricts the number of people who can use them. A genuinely practical four-seater could introduce Riversimple to a far wider audience.

Again, there is real substance behind the speculation. Riversimple's own proposed range includes a two-door, four-seat hatchback with a minimum 300-mile range and a targeted 0–60mph time of 10.5 seconds. The company indicates that its subscription and mileage charges would be about 5% higher than for the two-seater. If achievable, that's an intriguing trade-off for two extra seats.

And there's an encouraging new development. In 2026, Riversimple announced its leadership of the £1.7 million ZELLOR project, aiming to demonstrate a four-seat hydrogen-electric vehicle weighing less than 1,000kg and capable of more than 400 miles. 

Meanwhile, hydrogen passenger cars have not disappeared from the international picture. Toyota continues developing the Mirai, Hyundai has introduced a new-generation NEXO, and BMW is preparing a hydrogen-powered version of its next X5 for series production in 2028 using fuel-cell technology developed with Toyota.

These are much larger and heavier vehicles than Riversimple's designs, but they underline that fuel-cell development continues across the industry. Perhaps a tiny Welsh manufacturer could find its own place in that market.


The third TNY design is a compact, two-seat commercial van. We've retained the passenger car's front end and overall height while extending and squaring off the rear bodywork to create a more useful load space. A small van doesn't need sports-car acceleration or luxury equipment; for urban deliveries and local services, ease of use, running costs and availability often matter more.

Riversimple is already considering this category. Its official waiting list includes a small runabout van with the same projected range, performance and subscription pricing as the two-seat hatchback. Shared engineering could therefore become an important part of a future vehicle family, although Riversimple has not confirmed final production specifications, dimensions or payload capacities.

Hydrogen also has a foothold in British commercial transport. Northern Ireland manufacturer Wrightbus builds fuel-cell buses including the StreetDeck Hydroliner, with examples used in UK public transport.

Larger fleet operators can sometimes support dedicated refuelling facilities and predictable routes, something private motorists rarely can. A lightweight Riversimple van could suit that localised model, especially where other hydrogen vehicles already operate.

However, a bus depot's hydrogen pump is not automatically a public filling station, and hydrogen supply remains a major challenge. Fleet growth might help justify new infrastructure, but will not necessarily create a convenient national network for car drivers. That's why a regional deployment strategy may be a more realistic first step than an immediate nationwide launch.


And yet the Riversimple story reaches further back than the LIFECar. In 2004, Hugo Spowers was involved in the tiny, single-seat BOC Shell Eco-Marathon project, developed with BOC, siGEN, Shetland Composites and OScar Automotive. Looking at the little blue-and-white machine today, it seems almost impossibly distant from the more polished Rasas.

The figures remain remarkable: a vehicle weighing approximately 40kg, powered by a 25-watt hydrogen fuel cell, and engineered around a target efficiency exceeding 10,795mpg equivalent.

Riversimple has described a theoretical ability to travel around the world using the energy equivalent of just two gallons of fuel. That was a comparison illustrating its extraordinary efficiency ambitions, not a claim that the vehicle was a practical road car capable of such a journey.

It was an experiment, but an important one. The recurring Riversimple principles — minimise weight, reduce energy demand and rethink familiar automotive assumptions — were already visible more than twenty years ago.


For a company that has not yet become a mass-market carmaker, Riversimple has a surprisingly substantial history. It has created several generations of working hydrogen vehicles, developed an unusual low-power architecture, put Rasas into real-world trials and kept specialist engineering activity in Wales. 

There are also practical challenges to overcome. Battery-electric cars have moved into the mainstream, while hydrogen passenger vehicles remain a niche market. Producing, transporting and dispensing hydrogen all involve costs and energy use, while its environmental benefits depend on how the fuel is made.

Public hydrogen filling stations remain scarce across Britain. Refuelling in just three minutes is an attractive prospect, but a much wider infrastructure network will be needed to unlock the technology's full potential.

But it would be a mistake to confuse those obstacles with a lack of progress. Hydrogen is finding applications in some buses and other fleet vehicles, and manufacturers such as Toyota, Hyundai and BMW continue investing in fuel-cell technology.

Riversimple's particularly lightweight approach offers another possibility entirely: use much less hydrogen in the first place. With the ZELLOR project underway and three possible vehicle types outlined, there are still genuinely interesting chapters to be written.


From a 40kg economy experiment in 2004 to the Rasa, public trials and today's ambitions for more practical vehicles, Riversimple has followed a path very different from the rest of the industry. Our two-seat hatchback, four-seater and compact van are TNY Design Studio's interpretations of where that journey might lead, not previews of confirmed production models.

Yet the company itself is considering all three categories, and its latest engineering programme provides a reason to keep paying attention. Electric cars may dominate the headlines, but there could still be room for a small Welsh company prepared to approach hydrogen from an entirely different angle.

The real challenge now is turning decades of intriguing engineering into everyday vehicles that people can actually use.

items.title: Taking on the X5 – Mercedes' Next Generation of Luxury SUVs
items.summary: Mercedes-Benz helped shape the premium SUV market long before BMW joined the party. The original M-Class arrived in 1997, two years ahead of the first BMW X5, at a time when the Range Rover was still the established benchmark for luxury off-roaders. Originally known as the M-Class or ML, the model became…
items.content_html:
Mercedes certainly hasn't been standing still. Unveiled on 17 October 2026, the new all-electric Mercedes-AMG GT SUV delivers up to an extraordinary 1,153bhp, with a maximum WLTP range of around 435 miles and charging speeds of up to 710kW. It's a formidable new arrival that could challenge the performance end of BMW's electric SUV range.

However, BMW's fifth-generation X5 takes a broader approach, offering petrol, diesel, plug-in hybrid and fully electric powertrains, with a hydrogen fuel-cell version planned for 2028.

That leaves Mercedes needing more than an electric performance flagship to answer BMW's challenge. So, what should the next-generation GLE look like? TNY Design Studio explores three possibilities, starting with the conventional GLE SUV.


Across four generations, the M-Class and later GLE have become one of Mercedes-Benz's most important SUVs, with TNY estimating approximately 3.5 million sold worldwide since 1997. A fifth generation therefore has a difficult job: modernising an established favourite without losing its identity.

For our proposed 2028 GLE, TNY Design Studio has made one particularly significant departure. We've abandoned the distinctive rear quarter-window and C-pillar treatment that has been a defining feature of the M-Class since 1997, replacing it with a cleaner, more conventional glasshouse inspired by the latest GLC.

Combined with a more imposing front end, sharper detailing and a cleaner body design, our interpretation aims to bring the GLE into Mercedes' next design era. With BMW moving its new X5 closer to five metres in length, Mercedes has an opportunity to make its fifth-generation GLE feel like a genuine step forward, rather than another evolution of the familiar formula.


Since its introduction in 2015, the GLE Coupé has established itself as an important part of Mercedes-Benz's SUV family, offering a sportier alternative to the conventional GLE and a direct rival to BMW's X6.

However, Mercedes' more recent SUV designs haven't all enjoyed the same reception. The all-electric EQE SUV has struggled to establish itself in some markets, with its rounded, aerodynamically focused styling dividing opinion. The newly revealed Mercedes-AMG GT SUV suggests a change of direction, embracing a more striking, muscular and dynamic appearance.

For our proposed 2028 GLE Coupé, TNY Design Studio takes a slightly different approach. Rather than exaggerating the sloping roofline, we've introduced a more elegant, saloon-inspired rear profile, creating something between a traditional SUV Coupé and a raised luxury saloon.

The result is an interpretation that prioritises elegance over aggression, while retaining the road presence expected of a Mercedes-Benz luxury SUV.

Mercedes-Benz has never been afraid to experiment with its larger luxury vehicles. Introduced in 2005, the original R-Class combined elements of an estate car, MPV and SUV into something rather unusual. Offering six or seven seats, generous interior space and the comfort of a luxury saloon, it was intended to create an entirely new category of premium family transport.

Commercially, however, the R-Class never achieved the success Mercedes had hoped for. Sales disappointed in Europe and North America, although the model enjoyed a longer life in China.

Nevertheless, the R-Class demonstrated Mercedes' willingness to explore unconventional ideas within the potentially lucrative premium SUV market, rather than simply following established formulas.

Two decades later, with luxury SUVs more popular and diverse than ever, could Mercedes be tempted to experiment again?

If Mercedes-Benz was ever going to revisit the R-Class idea, now may be the time. When the original arrived, its blend of SUV, estate and MPV qualities felt unusual. Today, however, the market is far more open to experimental luxury vehicles, while premium MPVs have become a much more established part of the high-end family car market.

That creates an interesting opportunity for Mercedes. A modern successor could offer something genuinely different from the familiar large-SUV formula, combining the road presence buyers expect with greater cabin space, easier access and a more versatile interior.

Our proposed GLR keeps broadly similar dimensions to the original R-Class, preserving its long, substantial silhouette, but reinterprets the concept using Mercedes' modern design language. The result is less awkward and more cohesive, blending MPV practicality with the cleaner surfacing, sharper lighting and stronger front-end presence expected of a contemporary Mercedes-Benz.

Could this finally be the right time for Mercedes to try again?


BMW's latest X5 highlights the challenge facing Mercedes. What began as a straightforward rivalry between two large premium SUVs has developed into a much broader contest, encompassing SUV coupés, electric models and high-performance flagships.

With the fifth-generation X5 approaching five metres in length and offering an unusually broad range of powertrains, Mercedes needs to consider not only how its next GLE looks, but also where it fits within an increasingly competitive luxury SUV market.

So, how closely matched are the two manufacturers' existing line-ups?

Perhaps the biggest surprise is just how closely matched these models are. The outgoing BMW X5 is only 12mm longer than the current GLE, while the GLE Coupé and X6 are separated by just 20mm.

Although BMW's new X5 is growing, extra length alone won't define the next generation. Mercedes must find ways to make its luxury SUVs feel distinctive, rather than simply matching its rival's dimensions.

And as our final image illustrates, the next GLE could represent something more significant: a departure from almost three decades of familiar M-Class design.


For Mercedes-Benz, taking on the X5 shouldn't simply mean building a larger GLE. BMW's expanding range demonstrates how diverse the luxury SUV market has become, but Mercedes has the heritage and engineering expertise to respond in its own way.

Our proposed fifth-generation GLE brings a familiar favourite into a cleaner design era, while the GLE Coupé explores a more elegant alternative to the traditional SUV fastback. The GLR is perhaps the boldest proposal of all, reviving the versatility of the R-Class for a market that might finally appreciate it.

Whether Mercedes chooses evolution or something more adventurous, its next generation needs to offer more than just a new grille.

items.title: The Next Microcar Generation – Six Little Cars with Big Ambitions
items.summary: Microcars might occupy a small corner of Europe's automotive market, but their appeal is difficult to ignore. In 2025, France registered 24,919 new light quadricycles, while Italy recorded 17,989 light and heavy quadricycles, more than 72% of them electric. Their appeal lies in simplicity. Compact dimensions, low energy consumption and modest running…
items.content_html:
Chinese manufacturer Bontu is bringing its electric microcars to Europe, having introduced the range in Milan earlier this year. Among the newcomers is the BT09, a compact, affordable alternative to established models such as the Citroën Ami.

Measuring just 2,750mm long and 1,450mm wide, the BT09 comes in two versions. The two-seat L6e model has a 7.68kWh battery, offering a claimed 81-mile range and a 28mph top speed. A more capable four-seat L7e version increases battery capacity to 10kWh, range to approximately 93 miles and top speed to 47mph.

Italian pricing is expected to start around €9,500, making it an interesting proposition for budget-conscious buyers.

Stepping up from the smaller BT09, the Bontu BTE05 offers considerably more space and performance, potentially making it a more convincing alternative to a conventional city car.

Measuring 3,000mm long, 1,500mm wide and 1,630mm tall, the BTE05 is available with two or four seats. Buyers can choose between 13.9kWh and 18.1kWh LFP batteries, delivering claimed ranges of 106 and 138 miles respectively. Its 56mph top speed also makes it considerably more versatile than a typical 28mph microcar.

Equipment is surprisingly generous, including air conditioning, ABS, a driver's airbag and a 12-inch touchscreen.

European pricing has been estimated at €14,000–€17,000 (approximately £12,000–£15,000), although official prices remain unconfirmed. Bontu is establishing itself in Italy, but a British launch has yet to be announced.

Perhaps the most significant newcomer is the Dacia Hipster, a remarkably simple electric microcar designed to bring affordable motoring to a wider audience.

Measuring just 3,000mm long, 1,550mm wide and 1,530mm tall, the boxy Hipster manages four proper seats and a 70-litre boot, expanding to 500 litres with the rear seats folded. Weighing under 800kg, the concept is approximately 20% lighter than the Dacia Spring.

Reports suggest production could begin in China during 2027, with a 15kWh battery, approximately 20bhp and a targeted UK price below £10,000.

That could make the Hipster one of Britain's most affordable new electric vehicles, although production and pricing remain unconfirmed by Dacia. Its combination of four seats, clever packaging and potentially accessible pricing could make it a particularly important addition to the emerging L7e market.

Fiat's growing microcar ambitions now extend well beyond the familiar Topolino. The Italian manufacturer has three distinct approaches to micromobility: the two-seat Topolino, the three-wheeled Tris commercial vehicle and the four-seat Multiplina.

First revealed in July 2026 and subsequently displayed at the Paris Motor Show, the Multiplina takes inspiration from the original 1956 Fiat 600 Multipla, promising considerably greater practicality than its smaller siblings.

While the Topolino measures just 2,558mm long, offers 46 miles of range and is limited to 28mph, the Multiplina aims to accommodate four occupants within a body measuring under three metres. Developed around the L7e heavy quadricycle category, it could offer a 56mph top speed, greater power and a larger battery.

Production has been suggested for 2028, although Fiat is still working to reduce weight to meet quadricycle regulations. Pricing, battery specifications and UK availability remain unconfirmed.

Chinese newcomer Linktour is moving quickly into Europe, with its Alumi electric microcar already available in several continental markets. Following its British Motor Show debut in August 2026, the manufacturer is preparing to introduce three versions to the UK.

Measuring just 2,685mm long and 1,500mm wide, the two-seat Alumi features lightweight aluminium construction, frameless doors and a surprisingly contemporary interior.

The L6e Alumi and Alumi Pro offer a 7.2kWh battery, up to 75 miles of claimed range and a 28mph top speed. The more powerful L7e Elite+ increases capacity to 12.96kWh, delivering up to 112 miles and 56mph.

Belgian prices start at €10,490 for the Alumi and €14,990 for the Elite, equivalent to approximately £8,850 and £12,650. British prices and dealer availability remain unconfirmed, but Linktour's UK arrival appears increasingly close.


Spanish newcomer LIUX is taking an unusual approach to electric microcars, with its BIG making an international debut at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. Its most distinctive feature is a lightweight flax-fibre composite monocoque supported by a steel chassis, combining structural strength with reduced weight and environmental impact.

Measuring approximately 2,700mm long and 1,500mm wide, the two-seat L7e quadricycle weighs just 648kg and offers a surprisingly useful 240-litre boot. Two LFP battery options, 15kWh and 20kWh, promise 134 and 168 miles respectively under WMTC testing. Power comes from a 47bhp electric motor, with a 56mph top speed.

Production is planned for Spain, with deliveries expected during the first half of 2027. Prices should start below €18,000 (approximately £15,200), with Spain, France and Italy the initial markets.

UK availability remains unconfirmed, but the BIG's lightweight construction and impressive claimed efficiency make it one of Europe's more intriguing microcar newcomers.


For decades, Europe's microcar market was largely the territory of specialist manufacturers such as Aixam, Ligier and Microcar. More recently, mainstream manufacturers have joined the conversation, with the Renault Twizy, Citroën Ami, Opel Rocks Electric and Fiat Topolino introducing a new generation of buyers to tiny electric vehicles.

Now the segment appears ready for another wave of newcomers. Established carmakers are exploring greater practicality and affordability, while ambitious new manufacturers are introducing fresh designs, lightweight construction and increasingly capable electric powertrains.

For Britain, the question remains whether these vehicles can move beyond niche appeal and establish themselves as genuinely useful alternatives to conventional cars.

Not all six newcomers will necessarily reach UK showrooms, but the growing variety suggests that Europe's smallest vehicles could have a much bigger future than their modest dimensions might suggest.

items.title: Back to the Future – Reimagining the Mitsubishi i for Europe
items.summary: Few small cars have been as quietly ambitious as the Mitsubishi i. Launched in Japan with a rear-mounted petrol engine, it later became the i-MiEV, one of the earliest mass-produced electric cars. Two decades on, Mitsubishi is again leaning heavily on partnerships, with Renault-derived models underpinning much of its European range. Yet…
items.content_html:
The Mitsubishi i arrived in Japan in 2006 as a kei car, measuring just 3,395mm long and 1,475mm wide. Yet its rounded, almost futuristic body concealed some remarkably clever engineering.

By positioning a 659cc three-cylinder petrol engine ahead of the rear axle, Mitsubishi could push the wheels towards the corners, achieve a 2,550mm wheelbase and create surprisingly generous space for four occupants.

Rear-wheel drive, sophisticated De Dion rear suspension and a four-speed automatic made the i rather more interesting than the average city car. Britain even received the turbocharged petrol version in 2007, priced at around £9,000, although it remained a rare sight.

More importantly for Europe, its unconventional packaging provided the perfect foundation for the electric i-MiEV, which would later underpin the Peugeot iOn and Citroën C-Zero. (Image credit: Mitsubishi)

For our 2028 interpretation, TNY Design Studio imagines the Mitsubishi i returning on Renault's new Twingo E-Tech platform. At 3,790mm long and 1,720mm wide, it's noticeably larger than the original i-MiEV, but still compact. Our rendering retains the rounded cabin, distinctive proportions and playful character, updated with Mitsubishi's latest design language.

A Twingo-based i could inherit Renault's 27.5kWh LFP battery and 82PS motor, delivering up to 163 miles of WLTP range. That's a considerable improvement over the original i-MiEV's 16kWh battery, 67PS motor and 93-mile NEDC range, although the testing standards differ.

Practicality could improve too. Where the i-MiEV offered just 166 litres of boot space due partly to its rear-mounted powertrain, the Twingo provides up to 360 litres with its independently sliding rear seats pushed forward. A revived i could offer similar flexibility without sacrificing its city-friendly dimensions.



From the rear, our Mitsubishi i rendering retains one of the original car's most distinctive features: its high-mounted rear light clusters, now reimagined as slim vertical LED strips alongside the rear window. We've deliberately kept the tailgate and surrounding bodywork clean, preserving the simplicity that made the first-generation i so appealing.

There's also a logical place for it in Mitsubishi's European range. The Renault Clio-based Colt measures 4,053mm long, while the new electric Twingo is just 3,790mm, leaving a 263mm difference between the two.

A revived i could comfortably sit beneath the Colt, offering an affordable, four-seat electric city car without competing directly with its larger sibling. With Mitsubishi already relying on Renault for several European models, extending that relationship into the smallest segment seems an entirely plausible next step.


Renault's new Twingo is set to provide the foundations for a growing family of affordable electric city cars across the Renault-Nissan-Mitsubishi Alliance. The next-generation Dacia Spring and Nissan Pixo are both set to draw on the same architecture, with TNY having previously explored both models through our own Design Studio renderings.

Could Mitsubishi be the next brand to join this expanding family?

Our entry-level Mitsubishi i rendering imagines how an especially affordable version might look. Finished in non-metallic paint, with simple wheel trims, unpainted plastic mirrors and simplified lighting, it deliberately avoids unnecessary decoration.

For Mitsubishi, a revived i wouldn't need to be complicated or expensive. A straightforward, affordable electric city car could fill a noticeable gap in its European range, bringing back some of the originality and small-car ingenuity that made the first generation so interesting.


The original Mitsubishi i was a small car with big ideas, proving that clever engineering could make even the tiniest vehicles feel innovative. Its electric successor arrived ahead of its time, helping to lay the foundations for an industry-wide shift towards electrification.

Nearly two decades later, the market looks very different. Affordable electric city cars are finally beginning to gain momentum, and Mitsubishi already has access to the technology through its relationship with Renault.

A revived i wouldn't need to reinvent the electric car. It would simply need to be affordable, practical and distinctive, much like the original. For a brand rebuilding its European presence, perhaps looking back at one of its smallest creations could be a very sensible way forward.

items.title: Ditch the Diesel: 10 Fuel-Efficient Petrol Cars for £2,000
items.summary: With diesel prices reaching a record £2 a litre, the traditional advantage of running an economical diesel car is looking increasingly questionable. Older diesels might deliver impressive fuel economy, but expensive emissions equipment, potential reliability problems and rising repair costs can quickly wipe out any savings. Fortunately, petrol cars have come a…
items.content_html:
The Fiat 500 is perhaps the easiest choice for anyone wanting a small, economical petrol car without having to settle for something that looks old or outdated. Despite its age, the little Fiat still looks fresh, cute and distinctive, with a design that has aged remarkably well.

Of course, it won't suit everyone. There are only four seats, a tiny boot and limited rear passenger space, but for everyday commuting and town driving, there's plenty to like.

The dependable 1.2-litre petrol is our pick, with numerous examples available for under £2,000. That budget should comfortably secure a tidy pre-facelift example, potentially with around 100,000 miles on the clock, while the updated 2015 facelift is beginning to creep tantalisingly close to our price ceiling.

Around 50mpg is achievable in ordinary driving, and although the 1.3 MultiJet diesel can squeeze out a few more miles per gallon, higher diesel prices and potentially greater maintenance costs make the petrol particularly appealing.

Petrol power also suits the 500's lightweight, city-friendly character. The alternative 0.9-litre TwinAir is entertaining, with a surprisingly eager personality, but its real-world economy can tumble when you start enjoying the extra performance, something the characterful little engine actively encourages you to do.

Today, the Honda Civic is exclusively hybrid-powered, but things were very different twenty years ago. Back then, buyers generally gravitated towards the muscular 2.2-litre diesel or the conventional 1.4 and 1.8-litre VTEC petrol engines, leaving the unusual Civic IMA Hybrid somewhat overlooked.

That's good news for today's budget-conscious buyers, because the Civic Hybrid offers an appealing combination of family-friendly space, automatic transmission and impressive fuel economy.

Unlike the familiar Civic hatchback, the IMA came exclusively as a four-door saloon, with generous passenger accommodation, although its fixed rear seats make the boot less versatile. Its 1.3-litre petrol engine works alongside a small electric motor, delivering smooth, relaxed performance through a CVT automatic gearbox.

Our £2,000 budget should secure a 2008 example with over 100,000 miles, with around 50mpg achievable in favourable everyday driving. The biggest consideration is the ageing hybrid battery, which should be checked carefully before purchase, alongside the gearbox and service history.

The later Honda Insight arguably looks sharper and offers a more practical hatchback, but decent examples are harder to find within budget. Stretch to around £3,000, however, and you could even consider the distinctive CR-Z sports coupé, combining Honda's hybrid technology with a considerably more entertaining character.

When the Mitsubishi Mirage arrived in Britain, it wasn't exactly greeted with universal enthusiasm. Critics complained about its basic interior, uninspiring styling and rather unremarkable driving experience. It wasn't particularly fast, exciting or technologically advanced, and few considered it a serious rival to Europe's more polished superminis.

Yet time has been surprisingly kind to the little Mitsubishi. Its simple interior might have looked outdated when new, but there's relatively little technology to become obsolete or expensive to repair. More importantly, its dependable mechanicals and remarkably low running costs have aged considerably better than its original reviews might suggest.

The lightweight Mirage is exceptionally economical, with around 55mpg easily achievable in everyday driving from the 1.0-litre three-cylinder petrol engine. There's also more interior space than its compact dimensions suggest, with five doors, seating for five and reasonable practicality for such a small car.

Our £2,000 budget should secure a respectable example with around 80,000 miles, while higher-mileage cars can be found from approximately £1,000.

It might never win any awards for excitement, but as straightforward, dependable transport that costs very little to fuel, the Mirage makes considerably more sense today than its original reception suggested.

The second-generation Nissan Note is arguably one of the most sensible cars on our list, offering considerably more interior space than its compact footprint might suggest. It's easy to drive, economical, generally dependable and surprisingly practical, making it an excellent choice for families looking to keep motoring costs down.

Despite being barely larger than a conventional supermini, the Note offers generous rear legroom, excellent visibility and a useful 325-litre boot. Better-equipped versions even feature a sliding rear bench, allowing luggage capacity to expand to 411 litres when extra passenger space isn't needed.

Our £2,000 budget should secure a second-generation example from around 2014–2015, potentially with fewer than 100,000 miles on the clock. That's an impressive amount of car for the money, particularly considering how much room and versatility it offers.

The naturally aspirated 1.2-litre three-cylinder petrol is our preferred choice, offering straightforward mechanicals and respectable economy. Around 46 mpg is realistic in everyday driving, with 50mpg achievable on gentler journeys. Performance is modest, but perfectly adequate for ordinary commuting and family duties.

It might lack the charm of the Fiat 500 or the Mitsubishi Mirage's exceptional economy, but for buyers prioritising space, practicality and value, the Note is difficult to overlook.

The Peugeot 108 brought a welcome dose of maturity to the formula established by its predecessor, the 107. With smarter styling, a more modern interior and many examples equipped with a 7-inch touchscreen media system, it feels surprisingly contemporary for such an affordable little car.

Thanks to its lightweight construction, the 108 is remarkably nimble around town, even with the modest 1.0-litre three-cylinder engine. Around 55mpg is easily achievable, making it one of the most economical conventional petrol cars on our list.

There's also a punchier 1.2-litre PureTech option, offering noticeably stronger performance while still managing around 50mpg in real-world conditions. However, buyers need to be particularly careful with its oil-immersed timing belt, which can cause expensive engine problems if neglected. The Toyota-derived 1.0-litre is a safer bet, with a conventional timing chain and an excellent reputation for reliability.

Our £2,000 budget should secure an early 108 with around 100,000 miles, potentially including one of the better-equipped versions.

For those looking to spend even less, the older Peugeot 107 is every bit as economical, shares the dependable 1.0-litre engine and can be found from around £800. It feels considerably more basic, but represents exceptional value for anyone simply wanting cheap, dependable transport.

The third-generation Renault Twingo is one of the most interesting cars on our list, offering something genuinely unusual at this price point: a rear-mounted engine and rear-wheel drive. It's a layout more commonly associated with sports cars, yet here it creates one of the most manoeuvrable city cars ever made.

With an exceptionally tight 8.6-metre turning circle, the Twingo is brilliant around town, making narrow streets, awkward parking spaces and tight U-turns remarkably easy to negotiate. Unlike previous generations, this Twingo came exclusively with five doors, offering much better access to its surprisingly spacious cabin, although seating is limited to four.

The naturally aspirated 1.0-litre petrol is our economical choice, capable of returning around 50–55mpg in everyday driving. Performance isn't particularly exciting, but the Twingo's lightweight construction, compact dimensions and rear-wheel-drive layout make it an entertaining little companion.

Our £2,000 budget should secure a 2015 example with fewer than 90,000 miles, offering plenty of character for very little money. The more powerful 0.9-litre turbocharged version comes close to our budget, and its additional performance makes the Twingo feel particularly lively. However, real-world economy stands closer to 48mpg.


The SEAT Mii offers a sharper-looking alternative to the Volkswagen Up, sharing its mechanicals and efficiency while adding a little Spanish character. With SEAT's future now looking uncertain, it's easy to forget just how extensive the brand's range once was. When the Mii arrived, SEAT offered everything from conventional hatchbacks and estates to MPVs and even the Exeo saloon. The little Mii sat at the bottom of that range, providing compact, affordable transport.

Its 1.0-litre three-cylinder petrol engine came with either 60PS or 75PS, both offering respectable performance thanks to the car's lightweight construction. Around 50mpg is achievable with careful everyday driving, making the Mii a particularly economical choice for motorists looking to minimise their fuel bills.

Despite its compact dimensions, the Mii feels surprisingly mature on the road, with decent refinement, a well-built interior and reasonable passenger space, although it's strictly a four-seater.

Our £2,000 budget can secure an early example from around 2013–2014, with both three-door and more practical five-door versions worth considering. We'd favour the manual gearbox over the rather clumsy automated alternative.

The Mii enjoyed a relatively long production life and even became an electric car in 2019. Remarkably, the Mii Electric remains SEAT's only series-production battery-electric car. For anyone wanting dependable, economical motoring with a slightly more distinctive appearance than its Volkswagen sibling, the Mii is an excellent little car.

The Suzuki Celerio is another excellent example of how a little car can offer considerably more than its dimensions suggest. Combining almost Swift-like interior practicality with a footprint barely larger than the old Alto, it's a remarkably spacious, sensible and dependable little hatchback.

Its tall roofline, five-door body and surprisingly generous rear accommodation make it more versatile than many city cars, while the 254-litre boot is particularly impressive for something just 3.6 metres long. The interior is undeniably basic, but everything feels straightforward and designed to last.

However, fuel economy is where the Celerio really shines. Its lightweight construction and simple 1.0-litre three-cylinder petrol engine make it one of the most economical non-hybrid petrol cars of its generation. Around 50–55mpg is realistic from the standard engine, while the clever Dualjet version can achieve 60mpg with careful driving, without relying on expensive hybrid technology.

The Dualjet uses two fuel injectors per cylinder to improve efficiency, while retaining the simplicity of a naturally aspirated petrol engine. Both versions also benefit from timing chains rather than belts.

Our £2,000 budget can now secure an early example with fewer than 100,000 miles. It might not be the most exciting car in our selection, but for sheer economy, reliability and interior space, the Celerio is remarkably difficult to beat.

The second-generation Toyota Prius is arguably one of the most impressive cars on our list, combining excellent fuel economy with generous family accommodation, an automatic gearbox and Toyota's legendary reputation for reliability.

Its 1.5-litre petrol-electric hybrid powertrain has proven exceptionally dependable, with examples covering more than 400,000 miles demonstrating just how durable these cars can be. Around 55mpg is achievable with careful driving, with even better results possible in favourable urban conditions.

Unlike many of our smaller choices, the Prius is a genuinely spacious family car, offering five seats, a generous hatchback boot and a smooth, effortless automatic driving experience. It's particularly well suited to stop-start traffic, where its hybrid technology can make the biggest difference.

Our £2,000 budget should secure a second-generation example with around 160,000 miles, a figure that needn't be particularly concerning for a well-maintained Prius. However, the ageing hybrid battery deserves careful attention, especially on cheaper examples, where replacement costs could easily exceed the car's value.

For anyone wanting economical family transport without sacrificing space, comfort or automatic convenience, the Prius offers an extraordinary amount of car for £2,000.

The Vauxhall Astra is one of the biggest cars on our list, yet its surprisingly efficient 1.0-litre turbocharged three-cylinder petrol engine makes it an appealing alternative to an ageing diesel family hatchback. Around 46mpg is realistic in everyday driving, while 50mpg is achievable with a little care, particularly on longer journeys.

Much of that efficiency comes from General Motors' clever lightweight engineering. The Astra K shed up to 200kg compared with its predecessor, despite offering more interior space. The result was effectively Ford Focus practicality with a kerb weight approaching that of a Ford Fiesta, allowing its modest 105PS engine to deliver surprisingly capable performance.

Our £2,000 budget can secure a 2016 example with around 100,000–130,000 miles. These cars still look neat and modern, with comfortable interiors, respectable equipment levels and considerably better motorway refinement than many of the smaller city cars featured here.

The Astra is also available as a Sports Tourer estate, offering a generous 540-litre boot, expanding to 1,630 litres with the rear seats folded. However, equivalent 1.0-litre petrol estates generally start north of £3,000, putting them beyond our budget.

For buyers covering longer distances or regularly carrying passengers, the Astra makes a compelling case. It offers genuine family-car comfort, space and motorway ability while returning fuel economy that would once have been associated with a much smaller petrol car.

items.title: Taking Pride in the Little Things – Reimagining Kia’s Small Cars
items.summary: Over the past 20 years, Kia has transformed itself from a budget alternative into one of the world's most successful and increasingly desirable car manufacturers. The humble Picanto has played an important part in that journey, offering affordable, practical motoring to generations of buyers. Yet its future looks increasingly uncertain, with tightening…
items.content_html:
The Kia Stonic has effectively taken over from the discontinued Rio as Kia's affordable small-car offering, but beneath its recently refreshed styling lies a platform dating back to 2017.

Now more than nine years old, the Stonic is surely nearing the end of its current generation. Hyundai unveiled an entirely new Bayon at the 2026 Paris Motor Show, raising the question of how long Kia's closely related crossover can continue without a proper replacement.

With the EV2 establishing Kia's electric ambitions in this segment, TNY Design Studio imagines how a new-generation Stonic could bring fresh appeal to the petrol and hybrid market. (Image credit: Kia)


Hyundai's new Bayon has grown by 65mm to 4,245mm, and our imagined Stonic follows a similar direction. Stretching from today's 4,165mm to around 4,250mm, our rendering adopts a bolder, more substantial mini-SUV design, with stronger proportions and the confident styling increasingly expected of modern Kia crossovers.

That growth would also create more breathing room beneath the Stonic in Kia's range, opening the door for smaller, more affordable models. With the new Bayon set to introduce a full-hybrid powertrain, we would expect its Kia sister model to benefit from similar technology, alongside conventional petrol options.


Since arriving in 2004, the Kia Picanto has become a cornerstone of affordable motoring, accumulating almost 280,000 UK registrations across three generations. Still one of Britain's cheapest new cars, it remains surprisingly popular, with over 13,000 registered last year alone.

Yet its future is uncertain. With sister model Hyundai i10 leaving Europe and increasingly demanding emissions regulations threatening the Picanto's survival, could an electric successor provide the answer? (Image credit: Kia)


Back in July, TNY Design Studio explored the possibility of a Kia EV1, imagining a compact, slightly raised electric city car positioned beneath the new EV2.

Our original rendering combined practical, space-efficient proportions with Kia's increasingly distinctive design language, exploring how the brand could approach a value-focused electric city car.

Although Kia has yet to reveal the car officially, reports suggest a dedicated platform developed alongside Hyundai, a possible 2028 arrival and a target price of around £17,000. With competition in the affordable electric city-car market intensifying, the EV1 could prove crucial to keeping genuinely small, accessible models in Kia's European showrooms.


Kia already offers six models measuring between 4,150mm and 4,500mm: the Stonic, EV3, XCeed, Niro, EV4 hatchback and K4. Yet beneath them, the arrival of the 4,060mm EV2 highlights just how much room remains for smaller cars.

Even with our proposed Stonic growing to 4,250mm, Kia could comfortably accommodate three distinct models below 4,150mm. The rumoured EV1 would provide an affordable electric city car, while the EV2 covers the fast-growing compact SUV market.

But what about a more conventional supermini, offering a lower, sportier alternative to the Suzuki Swift and Vauxhall Corsa, just as the Rio once did? (Image credit: Kia)


The original Kia Pride holds a special place in the company's history, introducing British buyers to the brand in 1991. Developed by Mazda for Ford, and also sold as the Festiva and Mazda 121, it had surprisingly international roots.

Its budget pricing and sometimes cheap finishes made it feel rather low-rent at the time, but its clean, straight-edged design has aged remarkably well.

Kia hasn't forgotten its humble beginnings either. In 2024, the company celebrated its 80th anniversary with a one-off electric Pride, developed alongside British specialists Electrogenic. Could this overlooked little hatchback provide inspiration for Kia's next affordable supermini? (Image credit: Kia)


Interestingly, Kia has already confirmed plans for a new electric B-segment hatchback for Europe, suggesting the traditional supermini isn't entirely forgotten. Although its name and appearance remain a mystery, it presents an intriguing opportunity.

Our imagined Pride revival adopts a deliberately simple, retro-inspired design, following the approach taken by the Renault 5 and Fiat Grande Panda. Straight edges, squared-off proportions and clean detailing revisit the original Pride's character without appearing old-fashioned.

Compact, practical and potentially affordable, a modern Pride could restore something increasingly absent from Kia's European range: a conventional, desirable little hatchback without the bulk of an SUV.


Kia's small hatchback heritage stretches back 35 years in Britain, from the humble Pride through several generations of Rio, each reflecting the company's remarkable transformation. With a new generation of electric supermini now promised, the question is what direction Kia will take.

Will it embrace the sharp, futuristic styling of its latest electric models, or rediscover some of the simplicity and character of its earlier cars? Our design sketches explore the latter, bringing together elements of Kia's small-car history to imagine something familiar, yet thoroughly modern.


Kia has come a remarkably long way from the days when the Pride offered little more than entry-level, basic transport. Today, the brand has the design confidence, technology and increasingly strong reputation to make small cars genuinely desirable.

With the EV2 arriving, a smaller EV1 rumoured and a new electric hatchback already promised, the foundations of a comprehensive small-car family are beginning to take shape.

Our imagined Stonic, EV1 and Pride demonstrate how Kia could give each model its own identity, offering buyers a choice between practicality, affordability and character. As many manufacturers move upmarket, Kia has a rare opportunity to reconnect with the values that helped build its reputation: practical, desirable small cars that remain within reach of ordinary buyers

items.title: Market Watch: Ten Sensible Classics That Could Save You Money
items.summary: Classic cars aren't usually associated with sensible motoring. They're often regarded as expensive hobbies, requiring constant attention and substantial maintenance budgets. Yet some of Britain's forgotten family cars could offer a surprisingly affordable alternative to an ordinary used vehicle. For this edition of TNY Market Watch, we're exploring ten practical petrol-powered classics…
items.content_html:
Audi was already establishing its reputation for understated quality when the second-generation 80 arrived in 1978. Its clean, angular styling has aged particularly well, while the spacious interior and conventional four-door saloon layout make it a surprisingly practical classic.

Interestingly, some modern Audis have attracted criticism for excessive glossy plastics and screen-heavy dashboards, occasionally prioritising technology over traditional cabin quality. The B2 represents a different era, when straightforward controls, solid assembly and restrained design were central to Audi's appeal.

The 1.6-litre petrol with a manual gearbox is our preferred choice, offering adequate performance and real-world economy of around 32mpg. It's also mechanically straightforward, sharing various components with contemporary Volkswagen models, particularly the Passat, meaning some replacement parts remain relatively accessible. Corrosion and increasingly scarce model-specific trim and bodywork deserve attention, however.

Buyers should allow £4,000–£6,000 for a presentable example. Unlike newer used Audis, a well-bought B2 has already experienced most of its depreciation, with surviving examples becoming increasingly uncommon.

Choose a qualifying pre-1986 car and historic road tax costs nothing, with MOT exemption another potential saving. For someone covering relatively few miles each year, the Audi 80 offers genuine family-car practicality and the possibility of recovering much of its purchase price when the time comes to sell.


Few cars capture the spirit of affordable motoring quite like the Citroën 2CV. Introduced in 1948, it remained in production until 1990, an extraordinary 42-year career that made it one of France's most recognisable cars.

The later 2CV6 featured a 602cc air-cooled two-cylinder engine, offering a wonderfully characterful driving experience while potentially returning around 44mpg. Its remarkably soft suspension, simple mechanicals and surprisingly practical cabin make it an unusual but appealing classic.

The 2CV's philosophy never really disappeared. Citroën has repeatedly reimagined its combination of simplicity, comfort and unconventional design, from the C3 and C4 Cactus to the electric Ami. Now, an affordable electric successor is planned for 2028, ending a 38-year absence from showrooms.

We've allowed £5,000–£8,000 for a usable example, with a healthy selection of surviving cars and good parts availability through specialists. Rust remains an important consideration, so condition should take priority when choosing an example.

With the majority of 2CVs built before 1986, finding an example eligible for historic vehicle benefits shouldn't be difficult. Its enduring popularity, strong enthusiast following and distinctive character could also help protect against depreciation.


When the Austin Metro arrived in 1980, it was intended to become Britain's new Mini. Ironically, the original Mini would outlive it, remaining in production until 2000. Yet the Metro was a clever little car, combining compact dimensions, excellent packaging and affordable running costs at a time when imported superminis were becoming increasingly popular.

The MG Metro followed in 1982, bringing sportier styling, sharper handling and a lively 72bhp 1.3-litre petrol engine. Despite its performance, real-world economy could reach around 40mpg, making it surprisingly sensible transport.

Four usable seats, a practical hatchback boot and simple mechanicals add to its appeal. Rust and the condition of the Hydragas suspension deserve attention, although specialist support remains available.

We've allowed £4,000–£7,000 for a presentable example. With historic tax and MOT exemptions for qualifying cars, the MG Metro offers an entertaining alternative to conventional classics, with increasing rarity potentially helping to protect its value.


When the original Nissan Micra arrived in Britain in 1983, Japanese manufacturers were increasingly challenging Europe's established small-car favourites. The Micra demonstrated why, offering dependable, economical transport wrapped in a simple but cleverly packaged hatchback.

Its lightweight construction and 1.0-litre petrol engine made it particularly economical, with around 45mpg achievable in everyday driving. Performance was perfectly adequate for its intended purpose, while light controls, good visibility and compact dimensions made the Micra an excellent town car.

Despite its small footprint, the K10 provided usable rear seats and a practical boot. Straightforward mechanicals and Nissan's reputation for reliability add to its appeal, although rust and increasingly scarce bodywork components deserve attention.

We've allowed £3,000–£5,000 for a tidy early example. Qualifying cars benefit from historic road-tax and MOT exemptions, while the growing rarity of original K10s could help preserve their value. It's an unpretentious classic that still makes considerable financial sense.


The original Renault 5 was one of Europe's defining small cars, combining distinctive styling, clever packaging and excellent fuel economy. Introduced in 1972, its compact dimensions and comfortable suspension made it particularly well suited to Britain's towns and country roads.

The 1.1-litre is our preferred choice, offering simple mechanicals, usable rear seats and a practical hatchback boot. With real-world economy approaching 45mpg, running costs could be remarkably similar to the Nissan Micra we've just explored.

The relationship between these two small cars has since taken an interesting turn. In the 1980s, the Japanese-built Micra was an imported rival to the Renault 5. Today, their electric successors aren't simply close competitors; they share the same AmpR Small platform, battery options and much of their underlying engineering. Both are even manufactured at Renault's Douai factory in France, making the latest Micra effectively a French-built sister car with distinctive Nissan styling.

We've allowed £4,000–£6,000 for a usable original Renault 5. Rust and ageing bodywork deserve attention, although mechanical simplicity and enthusiast support remain appealing. With renewed interest following the electric revival, a carefully chosen original could also have encouraging prospects for retaining its value.


Few classic cars are quite as distinctive as the Saab 96. Its unusual rounded styling, front-wheel-drive layout and reputation for durability helped establish Saab as a manufacturer willing to do things differently. The model also enjoyed considerable success in international rallying, demonstrating its abilities in demanding conditions.

From 1967, the 96 adopted a Ford-derived 1.5-litre V4 petrol engine, replacing the earlier two-stroke unit. Producing around 65bhp, it offered respectable performance for the period, with real-world economy approaching 32mpg.

Despite its unconventional appearance, the Saab is surprisingly practical, providing four seats, a useful boot and excellent winter-weather capability. Its relatively simple engineering is another attraction, although corrosion and the availability of model-specific parts deserve consideration. Specialist support remains available through Saab enthusiasts.

We've allowed £5,000–£8,000 for a presentable example. With production ending in 1980, every surviving Saab 96 is now old enough to qualify for historic vehicle benefits. Its rarity, rallying heritage and unmistakable character could also help protect against depreciation, making it an appealing alternative to more conventional classics.


Toyota's reputation for reliability was already firmly established when the fifth-generation Corolla arrived in 1983. With its neat, angular styling, practical interior and straightforward engineering, the E80 offered British buyers a dependable alternative to increasingly sophisticated European family cars.

The move to front-wheel drive brought improved packaging, while the economical 1.3-litre petrol engine offered adequate everyday performance and the potential to return around 40mpg. Comfortable seating, good visibility and useful luggage space make it a surprisingly sensible choice for occasional family transport.

Toyota's reputation for mechanical longevity is reassuring, although decades of use mean individual condition matters far more than the badge. Rust deserves particular attention, while finding replacement body panels and original interior components can be challenging.

We've allowed £6,000–£8,000 for a tidy 1.3-litre example. Early E80 Corollas have become remarkably uncommon in Britain, with many disappearing long before achieving classic status. Their increasing rarity, combined with Toyota's enduring reputation for dependability, could make a well-preserved example a particularly appealing long-term purchase.


The Triumph Acclaim marked an unusual turning point for Britain's motor industry. Introduced in 1981, it was developed through a partnership between British Leyland and Honda, effectively bringing Japanese engineering to British production. Based on the Honda Ballade, it also became the last car to wear the Triumph badge.

Its 1.3-litre petrol engine produced around 70bhp, delivering respectable performance and real-world economy approaching 36mpg. Unlike many earlier British Leyland products, the Acclaim quickly earned a reputation for dependable engineering and straightforward ownership.

Four doors, comfortable seating and a useful boot make it a practical alternative to smaller classics, while its Honda-derived mechanicals offer reassuring simplicity. Rust and increasingly scarce bodywork and trim components deserve attention, although specialist support remains available.

We've allowed just £2,500–£5,000 for a presentable example, making the Acclaim one of our most affordable choices. Its unusual British-Japanese heritage, growing rarity and status as the final Triumph could help protect against depreciation, particularly as more enthusiasts rediscover this often-overlooked saloon.


When the second-generation Volkswagen Golf arrived in 1983, it built upon the original's success with a larger body, improved refinement and greater practicality. Its understated styling has aged particularly well, helping make this generation one of the most recognisable everyday classics.

While the GTI attracts much of the attention, the 1.6-litre GL offers a more affordable alternative. With around 75bhp and real-world economy approaching 34mpg, it provides perfectly usable performance, while five seats, a generous hatchback boot and comfortable suspension make it surprisingly suitable for regular journeys.

Mechanical simplicity and excellent parts availability are major attractions, with strong specialist support and a large enthusiast community. Rust and previous repairs deserve attention, particularly on cheaper examples.

We've allowed £3,500–£6,000 for a presentable early GL. With GTI values already firmly established, the more ordinary versions are increasingly attracting interest of their own. A well-preserved example could offer dependable classic motoring without the substantial premium associated with Volkswagen's famous hot hatch.


The Volvo 300 Series is one of our more unusual choices. Originally developed from a DAF project, it arrived in 1976 as the three-door 343, with the five-door 345 following in 1979. From 1983, both were sold under the simpler 340 name. Once a familiar sight on British roads, the 300 Series even appeared in the UK's top-ten sales charts during the 1980s.

The Renault-sourced 1.4-litre petrol engine offered straightforward mechanicals and real-world economy of around 34mpg. Unusually for an affordable family hatchback, the 300 Series featured rear-wheel drive, with manual versions positioning the gearbox at the rear for improved weight distribution. We'd choose the manual over the unconventional Variomatic automatic.

Comfortable seats, useful luggage space and reassuringly solid construction make these Volvos surprisingly practical classics. Rust deserves attention, while Renault-derived mechanical components can be easier to source than model-specific bodywork and trim.

We've allowed £3,000–£4,500 for a presentable example. Despite its former popularity, the 300 Series has become an increasingly rare sight, with surviving examples often overlooked in favour of more fashionable classics. That growing rarity could help protect against depreciation, making this unconventional Volvo a fitting conclusion to our ten sensible classics.

– These ten classics demonstrate that affordable motoring doesn't necessarily mean buying something modern. From the economical Nissan Micra to the characterful Saab 96, each offers a different combination of practicality, simplicity and classic appeal.

None is guaranteed to appreciate, and unexpected repairs can quickly outweigh savings on tax or depreciation. However, for motorists covering relatively few miles, choosing a well-maintained classic could provide something increasingly difficult to find in an ordinary used car: enjoyable ownership without the expectation of losing thousands of pounds in value.

Disclaimer: Prices, fuel economy figures and vehicle information are provided for general guidance and may vary. Historic tax and MOT exemptions are subject to eligibility, and all vehicles must remain roadworthy. Classic-car values are not guaranteed, and buyers should inspect vehicles carefully before purchasing.

items.title: Wet Belts: The Problems, the Prices and the Cars Worth Considering
items.summary: As manufacturers faced increasingly demanding emissions targets, even tiny improvements in engine efficiency became valuable. Compact three-cylinder engines spread from city cars into family hatchbacks, SUVs and even commercial vehicles, helped by turbocharging and increasingly sophisticated engineering. One of the technologies adopted to reduce friction and mechanical noise was the wet timing…
items.content_html:
Ford's 1.0-litre EcoBoost was an impressive piece of engineering when it arrived in 2012. Despite having just three cylinders and a tiny displacement, it offered lively performance, with outputs eventually reaching 138bhp in the Fiesta.

Official economy figures could approach 65mpg, although achieving anything close to this in everyday driving proved difficult. This wasn't a wet-belt problem, but rather a familiar characteristic of small turbocharged petrol engines, which became increasingly common across Europe.

Unfortunately, the EcoBoost's reputation would eventually become dominated by its oil-immersed timing belt. Designed to reduce friction and mechanical noise, the belt could deteriorate over time, particularly when exposed to degraded or unsuitable engine oil. Fragments of rubber could then accumulate around the oil-pump pickup, restricting lubrication and potentially causing serious engine damage.

For some owners, the consequences were expensive, with failures resulting in damaged turbochargers or even complete engine replacements. The problem became sufficiently well known that the once-celebrated EcoBoost developed an unfortunate reputation among used-car buyers.

Less obviously, the later Fiesta's naturally aspirated 1.1-litre Ti-VCT petrol also used a wet timing belt, meaning avoiding the turbocharged EcoBoost didn't necessarily mean avoiding the technology.


The 1.0 EcoBoost wasn't confined to the Fiesta. Ford fitted it to considerably larger models, including the Focus, Mondeo, C-Max and B-Max, alongside the EcoSport SUV and Transit Courier. That gave buyers the economy and relatively low emissions of a small petrol engine without necessarily sacrificing the practicality of a family car.

Fortunately, preventative wet-belt replacement isn't always as expensive as its reputation suggests. We've found independent garages across Britain advertising replacements for around £600, with some quoting even lower starting prices. Comprehensive packages can include both belts, fresh oil and filter, and oil-system cleaning. Owners should confirm exactly what's included before accepting a quote.

The EcoBoost's reputation has also created an interesting opportunity in the used-car market. We've found several 2013 Fiesta 1.0 EcoBoost examples with around 100,000 miles advertised for approximately £2,000, including the desirable 125PS version. That's a tempting price for a car with excellent road manners, a 0–62mph time of just 9.4 seconds and the potential to approach 50mpg with careful driving.

Many pre-April 2017 EcoBoost Fiestas also qualify for annual road tax of just £20. For buyers prepared to check the service history and budget for preventative maintenance, a well-kept example could represent considerably better value than its reputation might suggest.

But it wasn't the 1.0 EcoBoost where Ford's wet-belt story began. Back in 2007, Ford and Dayco introduced the world's first production automotive belt-in-oil system on the 1.8-litre TDCi diesel, replacing the chain previously used to drive its fuel-injection pump.

The engine appeared in the Focus, C-Max, Mondeo, S-Max and Galaxy, offering a useful middle ground between Ford's smaller 1.6 and more powerful 2.0-litre diesels. Often overlooked, the 125bhp Mondeo 1.8 TDCi offered respectable performance and real-world economy approaching 45–50mpg.

Unlike the later EcoBoost, the 1.8 retained a conventional dry camshaft timing belt, with its oil-immersed belt driving the injection pump instead.

Ford has since moved its revised 1.0 EcoBoost to chain-driven camshafts, including conventional petrol and mild-hybrid applications. Some versions still retain a wet oil-pump belt, however, meaning the transition away from the technology isn't quite as straightforward as it first appears.

Ford's use of wet timing belts didn't end with its smaller petrol engines. In 2016, the company introduced the 2.0-litre EcoBlue diesel, designed for considerably more demanding applications, including the Transit, Transit Custom and, from 2019, the Ranger pickup. The engine also found its way into passenger vehicles, including the Mondeo, Kuga, S-Max and Galaxy.

Unlike the tiny EcoBoost, the EcoBlue was developed with commercial use in mind, where high mileages, heavy loads and long working days are commonplace. Despite these tougher demands, Ford continued using an oil-immersed timing belt, alongside a separate wet belt driving the oil pump.

The consequences of deterioration can be particularly serious for commercial operators, with restricted oil flow potentially causing extensive engine damage and leaving a working vehicle off the road.

Replacement is also a more involved procedure. Access requires substantial dismantling, while the timing cover and sump must be carefully resealed. Some specialists allow a two-day turnaround to give the sealant sufficient curing time, adding to the inconvenience for businesses relying on their vehicles.

While wet-belt problems have become familiar territory for Ford owners, the technology also found its way into less obvious corners of the three-cylinder petrol market, including models from manufacturers with very different reputations for reliability.


Honda is a manufacturer traditionally associated with dependable engineering, and the tenth-generation Civic was no exception in many respects. Introduced in 2017, its entry-level 1.0-litre VTEC Turbo delivered 129PS, respectable performance and impressive fuel economy, making it an appealing alternative to the increasingly common small turbocharged engines from European manufacturers.

However, Honda also adopted an oil-immersed timing belt, introducing a potential weakness into an otherwise accomplished family hatchback. As with Ford's EcoBoost, belt deterioration can lead to restricted oil flow and potentially serious engine damage, making correct servicing and preventative replacement particularly important.

Unlike Ford, Honda fitted this engine to just one generation of the Civic in the UK, with a considerably smaller number of vehicles on the road. Reports of wet-belt failures do exist, but finding widespread owner complaints on the scale associated with Ford or Stellantis is considerably more difficult.

That doesn't necessarily make Honda's design more dependable. With a much smaller population of affected vehicles, there are fewer owners reporting their experiences, making meaningful comparisons difficult.

Honda ultimately discontinued the 1.0 VTEC Turbo when the eleventh-generation Civic arrived in 2022, replacing the petrol range with its e:HEV hybrid powertrain and leaving the wet timing belt behind.


While Honda's use of wet timing belts was limited to a single generation of the Civic, Stellantis took the technology considerably further. Its 1.2-litre PureTech three-cylinder petrol engine appeared across an enormous range of vehicles, initially from Peugeot and Citroën, before spreading to other brands within the expanding Stellantis group, including DS, Vauxhall and Jeep, exposing a wider range of buyers to the same potential problems.

At 1,199cc, the PureTech was also around 20% larger than Ford's 1.0 EcoBoost and many rival three-cylinder petrol engines. This extra capacity gave it an advantage in everyday driving, particularly in heavier vehicles where smaller turbocharged engines could struggle to match their impressive official economy figures. In many applications, the PureTech offered a convincing combination of performance, refinement and real-world fuel economy.

Unfortunately, the engine developed a reputation for premature wet-belt deterioration, with debris potentially restricting oil circulation and causing expensive mechanical damage. However, that doesn't make every PureTech a bad engine or every affected car a poor purchase.

As with the Ford, buyers should pay particular attention to servicing history, correct oil specifications and evidence of belt inspection or replacement. A neglected example could quickly become an expensive mistake, regardless of how attractive its asking price might appear.


As with Ford's EcoBoost, the PureTech's reputation has created some tempting opportunities in the used-car market. A well-maintained example can offer plenty of car for remarkably little money, and the Citroën C4 Cactus is a particularly good example.

We've found 2014–2015 Cactus 1.2 PureTech 110 models with fewer than 100,000 miles advertised for around £2,000. Weighing little more than a tonne, the Citroën offers lively performance, reaching 62mph in approximately 9.3 seconds, while potentially achieving 50mpg in everyday driving.

Maintenance needn't be expensive, either. Garages across the UK advertise wet-belt replacements for under £600, with some starting at £350, including parts, labour, oil and filter. This makes cheaper used examples more appealing, provided buyers check what's included.

The Cactus demonstrates what made the PureTech attractive: a lightweight, practical family car combining performance with economy. With a good service history and appropriate belt maintenance, its damaged reputation could make it a genuine used-car bargain.


Stellantis has, however, been gradually moving away from wet timing belts. Since 2023, the group has introduced a newer generation of its 1.2-litre three-cylinder petrol engine with a timing chain, progressively replacing the older PureTech design across its brands. The 1.2-litre 48V mild-hybrid powertrain has used a timing chain from the outset, combining the petrol engine with electric assistance and an automatic dual-clutch gearbox.

The transition hasn't happened overnight. Some conventional petrol models continued using wet belts alongside newer chain-driven versions, making it important for used-car buyers to check the exact engine rather than relying on registration year alone.

The arrival of STLA Medium-based models, including the latest Peugeot 3008 and Vauxhall Grandland, further illustrates the group's changing direction. Their newer hybrid and electric powertrains leave the original wet-belt PureTech arrangement behind.

After more than a decade of widespread use, wet timing belts are increasingly confined to older Stellantis engine generations and remaining applications. Yet millions of these vehicles will remain on the road for years, and for buyers willing to understand their maintenance requirements, some could still represent excellent value.


Volkswagen is another manufacturer with an interesting connection to wet belts. While the company has previously used oil-immersed belts to drive oil pumps in some of its diesel engines, its newer Ford-developed commercial vehicles have brought wet camshaft timing belts into the range.

The partnership began taking shape in 2020, with the second-generation Amarok arriving in 2023, followed by the latest Transporter in 2025. Both are Ford-based vehicles, with their 2.0-litre diesel models using Ford's EcoBlue engine and its wet timing belt.

For owners facing a wet-belt replacement, however, there's a potentially useful way to reduce the cost. We've found independent Ford specialists advertising comprehensive EcoBlue wet-belt replacements from around £800, approximately £200 less than advertised Volkswagen-specific services. Owners should confirm that the specialist accepts their Volkswagen model and that the quoted work is equivalent.

The Ford connection could also help owners save on other shared mechanical maintenance, rather than automatically turning to Volkswagen specialists for every repair.

It's an unusual arrangement that demonstrates how closely related modern vehicles can be beneath their badges. For existing Transporter and Amarok owners, understanding what's under the bonnet could make an expensive maintenance job considerably more affordable.

Wet timing belts were introduced with good intentions. By running the belt inside engine oil, manufacturers reduced friction, mechanical noise and, crucially, emissions at a time when every gram of CO₂ mattered. Unfortunately, real-world experience showed that the technology could be highly sensitive to servicing standards and oil quality.

Yet that doesn't mean every wet-belt car should be avoided. Millions remain on the road, and many have covered high mileages without issue. For used-car buyers willing to budget for preventative maintenance and verify a strong service history, some wet-belt-equipped cars now represent exceptional value.

Understanding the risks is ultimately more important than fearing the technology itself.

Buyers should verify service histories, confirm manufacturer recommendations and obtain written repair quotations before making decisions. TNY cannot guarantee vehicle reliability or future repair costs.
